content: The pain you feel when a stone falls on your foot is not the stone itself. Similarly, your opinion of a politician, whether favorable or unfavorable, is not the politician. A metaphorical representation of a concept is not the concept itself. These distinctions are crucial because failing to differentiate between the representation and the reality can limit one’s understanding and cognitive abilities. Alfred Korzybski argued that many people confuse maps with territories in this sense. His famous dictum, The map is not the territory, is a foundational principle in General Semantics and is also applied in neuro-linguistic programming (NLP). This principle emphasizes that individuals do not have direct access to absolute reality. Instead, they only have access to their subjective beliefs and interpretations of reality, which they have constructed over time. Therefore, it is essential to recognize that a person’s beliefs about reality (the map) are not the same as reality itself (the territory). Gregory Bateson, in his essay Form, Substance, and Difference from Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972), elaborates on the inherent impossibility of fully knowing the territory. Any understanding of the territory is based on representations, which are themselves filtered through human perception and tools. For example, a map is a representation of what someone perceived and recorded, but as one traces this process back, it leads to an infinite regress of representations. The actual territory never fully enters the process because it is always mediated by representation. Bateson describes this as a mental world composed of maps of maps, extending infinitely. Bateson also highlights that the utility of a map does not necessarily depend on its literal accuracy but rather on its structural analogy to the territory for a specific purpose. He explores this idea further in his essay The Theology of Alcoholics Anonymous, where he suggests that a metaphorical map involving spirits could be just as effective for public health as one involving microbes, depending on the context. Jorge Luis Borges, in his short story On Exactitude in Science, humorously illustrates the futility of a perfectly accurate, one-to-one map. He describes a fictional empire where cartographers create a map the size of the empire itself, matching it point for point. Over time, this map becomes useless and is abandoned, left to decay. Borges uses this story to highlight the absurdity of attempting to create a map that is indistinguishable from the territory it represents. Josiah Royce, in The World and the Individual (1899), presents a philosophical conundrum about maps within maps. He imagines a perfectly detailed map of England that includes a map of the map, which in turn includes a map of the map of the map, and so on, leading to infinite regress. This recursive structure raises questions about the nature of representation and reflection. Royce’s thought experiment suggests that the act of reflection is an enduring capability of the human mind, not merely a fleeting act of self-examination. Edmund Husserl referred to this reflective ability as the transcendental ego, the mind’s capacity to abstract and understand itself. Standing between two mirrors, one can see an infinite series of reflections. However, one is not deceived into believing these reflections represent an infinite number of actual selves. Instead, one understands that the reflections are merely the result of mirrors facing each other. Similarly, fictional characters can reflect upon themselves or their stories without implying that the reader or spectator is also fictional. This capacity for abstraction and self-reflection is a uniquely human trait. Neil Gaiman retells a parable in Fragile Things to illustrate the relationship between storytelling and reality. He explains that the best way to describe a story is by telling it. The act of storytelling is both a balancing act and a dream. The more accurate a map becomes, the more it resembles the territory. However, a perfectly accurate map would be indistinguishable from the territory itself, rendering it both perfectly accurate and perfectly useless. Jean Baudrillard, in Simulacra and Simulation, argues that the development of electronic media has blurred the line between map and territory. In the age of simulation, representations no longer refer to a reality or substance. Instead, they generate a hyperreal, a reality without origin or reference. In this framework, the map precedes and creates the territory, reversing the traditional relationship. René Magritte’s painting The Treachery of Images illustrates the idea that perception mediates between reality and ourselves. The painting depicts a pipe with the caption Ceci n’est pas une pipe (This is not a pipe), emphasizing that the image is merely a representation, not the object itself. This concept also appears in discussions of exoteric and esoteric knowledge. Exoteric concepts can be fully conveyed through language and descriptors, such as mathematics. In contrast, esoteric concepts require direct experience for full understanding. For example, someone who has never tasted an apple cannot fully grasp its flavor through language alone; only by eating an apple can they truly understand the experience. Lewis Carroll humorously addresses this idea in Sylvie and Bruno (1889), where he describes a fictional map with a scale of one mile to one mile. A character notes the impracticality of such a map and suggests using the country itself as its own map. Joan Robinson, an economist, similarly critiques overly detailed models, stating that a model accounting for every variation of reality would be as useless as a one-to-one scale map. Korzybski’s insights about the map and the territory have influenced various fields, including surrealist art, literature, and philosophy. For instance, Jan Bucquoy’s comic Labyrinthe explores how maps cannot guarantee finding one’s way because the accumulation of events can alter one’s perception of reality. J.Z. Smith, a historian of religions, further explores these ideas in his book Map is Not Territory: Studies in the History of Religions (1978).
